entries.71.1: Then in the twelfth year Shatrughna wished to go to Ayodhya, which Rama guarded, with few servants and a small force following him.
entries.71.2: Turning back his ministers and the chief men of his host, he went with the finest horses and a hundred chariots.
entries.71.3: And having made seven or eight measured halts, that greatly renowned delight of the Raghus came to Valmiki's hermitage and lodged there.
entries.71.4: Then that bull among men saluted Valmiki's feet and took from the sage's hand water for the feet, the guest-offering and the rites of hospitality.
entries.71.5: And there the sage told the great-souled Shatrughna tales of many kinds and most sweet, by the thousand.
entries.71.6: And the sage spoke a word concerning the slaying of Lavana: 'A most hard deed was done by you in slaying Lavana.
entries.71.7: 'Many kings, gentle one, of great strength were slain by Lavana with their forces and their mounts as they fought, mighty-armed one.
entries.71.8: 'And that sinful one was slain by you in play, bull among men; and the fear of the world there has been quieted by your splendour.
entries.71.9: 'The dreadful slaying of Ravana was done with a great effort; but this great deed was done by you without effort at all.
entries.71.10: 'And a joy beyond compare arose in the gods at Lavana's death; and what pleases all beings and the world was done.
entries.71.11: 'And I saw that battle as it truly was, bull among men, seated in Vasava's hall, Raghava.
entries.71.12: 'And in my heart too, Shatrughna, there is the highest joy. I shall smell your head; this is the highest way of affection.'
entries.71.13: Having spoken thus and smelt Shatrughna's head, the great sage performed the rites of hospitality for him and for those who followed at his feet.
entries.71.14: And that best of men, having eaten, heard at that hour the supreme sweetness of song — the story of Rama, in due order.
entries.71.15: Joined with string and rhythm, made with the three seats of utterance, in perfect speech, endowed with all the marks and joined with even measure, he heard the story of Rama at that hour, as it had been wrought before.
entries.71.16: And hearing those syllables that were true and told the events as they had been of old, that tiger among men lost his senses, his eyes filled with tears.
entries.71.17: And senseless as it were for a moment, sighing again and again, he heard in that song what had come to pass as though it were happening then.
entries.71.18: And those followers of the king, hearing that wealth of song, bent their faces down and grew wretched and said, 'It is a marvel.'
entries.71.19: And the soldiers there spoke to one another: 'What is this, and where are we? Is this the seeing of a dream?
entries.71.20: 'That matter which we saw before we hear again here in the hermitage. What is this? Is it a dream, or has the fortune of a song been bound about us?'
entries.71.21: Coming to the highest wonder, they said to Shatrughna: 'Ask, best of men, ask Valmiki the bull among sages.'
entries.71.22: But Shatrughna said to them all, filled as they were with curiosity: 'Soldiers, it is not fitting for us to ask such things here.
entries.71.23: 'Marvels of many kinds happen here in this sage's hermitage; but it is not right out of curiosity to enquire of that great sage.'
entries.71.24: Having spoken this word to his soldiers, that delight of the Raghus saluted the great sage and went then to his own lodging.
entries.72.1: As that tiger among men lay down, sleep did not come to him, for he was thinking upon that unmatched song of Rama, full of many meanings.
entries.72.2: Hearing that most sweet sound joined with string and rhythm, the night passed swiftly for the great-souled Shatrughna.
entries.72.3: When that night was over, having done the rites of the forenoon, Shatrughna with joined palms said this to the bull among sages:
entries.72.4: 'Venerable one, I wish to see Raghava, the delight of the Raghus. I wish to have your leave, and the leave of these of strict vows.'
entries.72.5: As Shatrughna, scorcher of foes, spoke thus, Valmiki embraced that Raghava and gave him leave to go.
entries.72.6: And saluting that best of sages, he mounted his shining chariot and went swiftly to Ayodhya, eager to see Raghava.
entries.72.7: And that glorious delight of the Ikshvakus entered the lovely city, and that mighty-armed one entered where Rama of great splendour was.
entries.72.8: And he saw Rama in the midst of his ministers, his face like the full moon, as the thousand-eyed one is seen in the midst of the immortals.
entries.72.9: Saluting that great soul who blazed as it were with splendour, he said with joined palms to Rama of true valour:
entries.72.10: 'Great king, all that was commanded I have done. That sinful Lavana is slain, and his city is settled.
entries.72.11: 'These twelve years have passed without you, delight of the Raghus. I have no heart to dwell apart from you, king.
entries.72.12: 'Show me favour, Kakutstha of measureless valour. Like a calf without its mother, let me not stay away long.'
entries.72.13: As Shatrughna spoke thus, Rama embraced him and said: 'Do not give way to despair, hero; this is not the conduct of a kshatriya.
entries.72.14: 'Kings do not sink down in living abroad, Raghava. The people are to be guarded by us according to the law of the kshatriya, Raghava.
entries.72.15: 'From time to time, hero, come to look upon Ayodhya and upon me, best of men; and then you shall go again to your own city.
entries.72.16: 'And you are dearer to me than my own breath, and of that there is no doubt; yet the guarding of the kingdom must certainly be done.
entries.72.17: 'Therefore stay here, Kakutstha, and dwell here seven nights; afterwards you shall go to Mathura with your servants and forces and mounts.'
entries.72.18: Hearing that word of Rama's, joined with dharma and coming from his heart, Shatrughna said only 'Very well,' in a wretched voice.
entries.72.19: And having dwelt there seven nights at Raghava's command, that Kakutstha, that great bowman, made ready to go.
entries.72.20: And taking leave of the great-souled Rama of true valour, and of Bharata and Lakshmana, he mounted his great chariot.
entries.72.21: And followed a long way by the great-souled Lakshmana and by Bharata, Shatrughna went swiftly then to his city.
entries.73.1: Having sent Shatrughna on his way, Raghava with his two brothers took his pleasure in happiness, guarding the kingdom in dharma.
entries.73.2: Then after some days an aged brahmin of the countryside came to the door of the royal house, carrying his dead child.
entries.73.3: Weeping and uttering words of many kinds full of love and sorrow, again and again he said, 'My son, my son,' and spoke this word:
entries.73.4: 'What ill deed did I do before in another body, that I see you, my only son, gone to destruction?
entries.73.5: 'A child not yet come to youth, only five thousand years old, come to his end out of season, to my sorrow, little son.
entries.73.6: 'In a few days I too shall go to my end, and there is no doubt of it — I and your mother both, for grief of you, little son.
entries.73.7: 'I do not remember an untruth spoken, nor do I remember any harm done; I do not remember any sin done to any living creature.
entries.73.8: 'By what ill deed then has this son of mine, a child still, gone to Vaivasvata's abode without performing the rites for his father?
entries.73.9: 'I have never seen or heard before a thing so dreadful to look upon — the death of those whose hour has not come, as here in Rama's realm.
entries.73.10: 'There is some great fault in Rama, and of that there is no doubt, since death has come thus to children who dwell in his realm.
entries.73.11: 'For children who dwell in other realms have no fear of death. Bring him back to life, king — this child gone under death's power.
entries.73.12: 'Or I shall die at the door of the royal house with my wife, like one with no protector; and then, Rama, take the guilt of a brahmin's death upon you and be happy.
entries.73.13: 'With your brothers, king, you shall gain a long life. We have dwelt happily in this kingdom of yours, one of great strength.
entries.73.14: 'But now this has fallen upon us who stand within your rule, Rama; having come under the power of time, our happiness is little indeed.
entries.73.15: 'Now the realm of the great-souled Ikshvakus is without a protector; for having Rama as lord here, the killing of children is a certainty.
entries.73.16: 'By the faults of a king the people perish, being not guarded according to the law; and when a ruler is of ill conduct, men die out of season.
entries.73.17: 'Or when men do what is unfitting in the cities and the countryside and there is no protection, then the fear that time makes comes upon them.
entries.73.18: 'It is plain that there will be a fault in the king, and there is no doubt of it, in the city or in the countryside; and hence this slaying of a child.'
entries.73.19: Thus with words of many kinds, pressing the king again and again, burnt with sorrow, he clasped that son of his to him.
entries.74.1: Raghava heard all that pitiful lament of the brahmin, full of sorrow and grief.
entries.74.2: And burnt with sorrow he called those ministers of his, and Vasishtha and Vamadeva, and his brothers with the men of the guilds.
entries.74.3: Then eight twice-born ones were brought in with Vasishtha, and they said to that king who was like a god, 'May you prosper.'
entries.74.4: Markandeya and Maudgalya, Vamadeva and Kashyapa, Katyayana and Jabali, Gautama and Narada — all these bulls among the twice-born were seated upon the seats.
entries.74.5: Having saluted the great sages who had come, with joined palms, and the ministers and the men of the guilds each as befitted him and according to their liking,
entries.74.6: Raghava told the whole matter to all those seated there of blazing splendour: 'This brahmin presses me hard.'
entries.74.7: Hearing that speech of the wretched king, Narada answered the lord of men with an auspicious word in the presence of the sages:
entries.74.8: 'Hear, king, how the destruction of that child came about out of season; and hearing it, do what is to be done, delight of the Raghus.
entries.74.9: 'Long ago in the Krita age, king, the brahmins alone were ascetics; and in that age, king, no one who was not a brahmin was an ascetic in any way.
entries.74.10: 'In that age, blazing and made of Brahman and uncovered, all beings were born deathless and long of sight.
entries.74.11: 'Then came the age named Treta, of men endowed with bodies; and there kshatriyas were born, joined with the fullness of penance.
entries.74.12: 'In valour and in penance they were greater in their former birth — those great-souled men who were in the Treta age.
entries.74.13: 'And all that was brahmin and kshatriya, both what went before and what came after, was in both those ages joined with an equal power.
entries.74.14: 'And seeing no further distinction among them, they established there the accepted ordering of the four classes.
entries.74.15: 'In that age, blazing and made of dharma and uncovered, unrighteousness let fall one foot upon the face of the earth.
entries.74.16: 'And being joined with unrighteousness, splendour became dulled.
entries.74.17: 'That craving of the men of old, and that thick stain of passion, became the thing called falsehood, and set a foot upon the face of the earth.
entries.74.18: 'And falsehood having set down one foot out of unrighteousness, thereafter the fixed limit of life was made manifest as before.
entries.74.19: 'And when falsehood and unrighteousness had fallen upon the face of the earth, the world did only what was auspicious and held to truth and dharma.
entries.74.20: 'And in the Treta age the brahmins and kshatriyas performed penance, all of them; and the other men gave service.
entries.74.21: 'That highest dharma of theirs came to the vaishya and the shudra; and the shudras above all performed the honouring of all the classes.
entries.74.22: 'In this interval, best of kings, in unrighteousness and in falsehood, the men of old fell greatly into decline.
entries.74.23: 'Then unrighteousness set down a second foot; and thereafter the name Dvapara arose for that age.
entries.74.24: 'And in that age called Dvapara, as it moved toward its ending, unrighteousness and falsehood grew, bull among men.
entries.74.25: 'In that age reckoned as Dvapara, penance entered among the vaishyas; and through three ages penance entered three classes in order.
entries.74.26: 'Through three ages dharma was appointed for three classes; and the shudra does not obtain dharma by the ordering of the ages, bull among men. One of a lower class, best of kings, is now performing a very great penance.
entries.74.27: 'Penance shall be performed in a shudra womb in the age of Kali; but in the Dvapara, king, it is the highest unrighteousness for one of shudra birth.
entries.74.28: 'And such a one of great penance is now upon the border of your realm, king, and today that evil-minded one performs austerity; and by that came this slaying of a child.
entries.74.29: 'For whatever man of evil mind does unrighteousness or what should not be done in a king's realm, and does that which is the root of misfortune, in the city or elsewhere — he goes swiftly to hell, and that king with him, and there is no doubt of it.
entries.74.30: 'Of what is studied and what penance is done and what good work is performed, a king who guards his people in dharma has a sixth part.
entries.74.31: 'And if he is not the enjoyer of that sixth part, how does he guard the people?
entries.74.32: 'Therefore do you, tiger among men, search out your own realm; and where you see the ill deed, there make your effort.
entries.74.33: 'If this is done, best of men, there shall be an increase of dharma and a lengthening of the life of men; and this child too shall live.'
entries.75.1: Hearing that word of Narada's, full of nectar, he felt a joy beyond compare and said this to Lakshmana:
entries.75.2: 'Go, gentle one, and comfort that best of the twice-born, that man of good vows; and have the body of the child laid in a vessel of oil.
entries.75.3: 'With fragrances most excellent and with sweet-smelling oils, let it be so arranged, gentle one, that the child does not decay.
entries.75.4: 'Do so that the body of the child, being guarded, shall come to no ruin or dissolution, so that what remains to be done may be done.'
entries.75.5: Having so instructed Lakshmana of auspicious marks, that greatly renowned Kakutstha thought upon the Pushpaka, 'Come.'
entries.75.6: And knowing his intent, the Pushpaka adorned with gold came in a moment into Raghava's presence.
entries.75.7: And bowing low it said, 'Here I am, lord of men; I stand at your will, mighty-armed one, your servant come before you.'
entries.75.8: Hearing that fair speech of the Pushpaka, that lord of men saluted the great sages and mounted the chariot.
entries.75.9: Taking his bow and quiver and his sword of shining splendour, and leaving in the city those two heroes, Sumitra's son and Bharata,
entries.75.10: he went to the western quarter, searching here and there; and then that glorious one went to the northern quarter, which Himavat encircles.
entries.75.11: And not seeing there even the least ill deed, that lord of men looked also over all the eastern quarter,
entries.75.12: pure in its conduct and spotless as the surface of a mirror; and that mighty-armed lord of men, standing in the Pushpaka, looked upon it.
entries.75.13: Then that delight of the royal sages passed to the southern quarter, and upon the northern side of Shaivala he saw a very great lake.
entries.75.14: And in that lake the glorious Raghava saw an ascetic performing a very great penance, hanging with his head downward.
entries.75.15: And Raghava came to him as he practised that highest penance and said this word: 'You are blessed, holder of good vows.
entries.75.16: 'In what womb were you born, you who are grown in penance and firm in valour? Out of curiosity I ask you; I am Rama, the son of Dasharatha.
entries.75.17: 'What is the thing you desire — the gaining of heaven, or something beyond? What is the boon you rest upon, for whose sake you perform this most hard penance? I wish to hear, ascetic, upon what you have leaned in doing this austerity.
entries.75.18: 'Are you a brahmin — may it be well with you — or are you a kshatriya hard to conquer? Or a vaishya of the third class, or a shudra? Speak the truth.'
entries.75.19: Being addressed thus by that lord of men, he bent his head down and told that son of Dasharatha, that bull among kings, his birth and the cause for which his penance was undertaken.
entries.76.1: Hearing that word of Rama, whose deeds are done without effort, he bent his head down and spoke this word:
entries.76.2: 'I am born of a shudra womb, Shambuka by name. I seek godhead in this very body, Rama of great renown.
entries.76.3: 'I do not speak falsely, Rama; it is out of a wish to win the world of the gods. Know me for a shudra, Kakutstha, who has undertaken a fierce penance.'
entries.76.4: As that shudra was speaking, Raghava drew from its sheath his spotless sword of shining splendour and struck off his head.
entries.76.5: When that shudra was slain, the gods with Indra and with Agni at their head praised Kakutstha again and again, crying, 'Well done, well done.'
entries.76.6: And there was a great rain of divine and most fragrant flowers, loosed by the wind, that fell upon every side.
entries.76.7: And the gods, well pleased, said to Rama of true valour: 'This work of the gods has been well done by you, gentle one of great mind.
entries.76.8: 'Receive a boon, gentle one, whatever you desire, subduer of foes. For this shudra could have no share in heaven, delight of the Raghus, but for what you have done.'
entries.76.9: Hearing the gods' speech, Raghava with full attention said with joined palms to the thousand-eyed Purandara:
entries.76.10: 'If the gods are pleased with me, let that brahmin's son live. Grant me this boon, which is my highest desire.
entries.76.11: 'It was by a fault of mine that he went — that only son of a brahmin, taken by time to Vaivasvata's abode before his hour.
entries.76.12: 'Bring him back to life; may it be well with you. You should not make me false, for I promised the brahmin, "I shall bring your son to life."'
entries.76.13: Hearing that word of Raghava's, those best of the wise, the gods, answered Raghava gladly, being filled with pleasure:
entries.76.14: 'Be free of care, Kakutstha. That child on this very day has come again to life and is joined once more with his kinsmen.
entries.76.15: 'In the very moment, Kakutstha, in which this shudra was struck down, in that same moment the child was joined again with life.
entries.76.16: 'Fare well; may it be well with you. Let us go, bull among men; we wish to see the hermitage of Agastya, Raghava.
entries.76.17: 'For the consecration of that brahmarshi of great splendour is complete; the twelfth year has passed while he lay upon a bed of water.
entries.76.18: 'Let us go there, Kakutstha, to greet the sage. Come you also — may it be well with you — to see that best of sages.'
entries.76.19: And the delight of the Raghus, having promised the gods 'So be it,' mounted that chariot the Pushpaka, adorned with gold.
entries.76.20: Then those gods went in their chariots of wide extent, and Rama too followed swiftly to the penance-grove of the pot-born.
entries.76.21: Seeing the gods arrived, Agastya, that treasury of penance, that soul of dharma, honoured them all without distinction.
entries.76.22: Then, receiving that honour and honouring the great sage in return, the thirty went gladly with their followers to the vault of heaven.
entries.76.23: When they had gone, Kakutstha came down from the Pushpaka and saluted Agastya, best of sages.
entries.76.24: Saluting that great soul who blazed as it were with splendour and receiving the highest hospitality, that lord of men sat down.
entries.76.25: And the pot-born of great splendour and great penance said to him: 'Welcome to you, best of men; by good fortune you are come, Raghava.
entries.76.26: 'You are held in high honour by me, Rama, for your many excellent virtues; you are a guest to be worshipped and are always in my heart.
entries.76.27: 'The gods indeed tell of you as having come after slaying the shudra; and by the dharma of the brahmin his son was brought to life by you.
entries.76.28: 'Stay here this night in my presence, Raghava; and at dawn you shall go by the Pushpaka to your city.
entries.76.29: 'For you are the glorious Narayana, and in you all is established. You are the lord of all the gods; you are the eternal Person.
entries.76.30: 'And this ornament, gentle one, was made by Vishvakarma, divine and of divine form, blazing with its own splendour. Receive it, Kakutstha; do what pleases me, Raghava.
entries.76.31: 'For in the giving again of what has been given a very great fruit is spoken of. And you are able to bear it, and so are the Maruts with Indra among them.
entries.76.32: 'You are able to carry across even the dwellers in heaven with Indra; therefore I shall give it in due form. Receive it, lord of men —
entries.76.33: 'this divine ornament of many hues, blazing like the sun.'
entries.76.34: Then that great warrior of the Ikshvakus, Rama, best of the wise, remembering the law of the kshatriya, said to that great soul:
entries.76.35: 'This taking of a gift, venerable one, is unblamed for a brahmin. How shall I, being a kshatriya, receive it, bull among brahmins?
entries.76.36: 'You should tell me why it is given by a brahmin in particular.' Being addressed thus by Rama, the great sage answered:
entries.76.37: 'In the Krita age of old, Rama, in the age that was made of Brahman, all creatures were without a king, though Shatakratu was king of the gods.
entries.76.38: 'Those creatures ran to the lord of the gods of gods for the sake of a king: "God, Shatakratu was set as king by you for the gods.
entries.76.39: '"Give us too, lord of the worlds, a bull among men for our king, to whom we may offer worship and, with our sins shaken off, may walk. We shall not dwell without a king; this is our fixed resolve."
entries.76.40: 'Hearing the speech of the creatures and settling that highest matter,
entries.76.41: 'Brahma, best of the gods, called all the guardians of the world with Vasava and said, "Give portions of your splendour."
entries.76.42: 'Then all the guardians of the world gave portions of their own splendour; and Brahma then created Kshupa, from whom King Kshupa was born.
entries.76.43: 'And Brahma joined him with the portions of the guardians of the world; and then he gave Kshupa to those creatures as their king and lord.
entries.76.44: 'And with Indra's portion the king commanded the earth; and with Varuna's portion the ruler nourished his body.
entries.76.45: 'With Kubera's portion he gave wealth to them; and with that portion which was Yama's he ruled the people.
entries.76.46: 'Therefore, best of men, delight of the Raghus, receive it by that portion which is Indra's; may it be well with you, and it is for my crossing over, lord.'
entries.76.47: Hearing that most righteous word of the sage, Rama received that finest ornament from the sage.
entries.76.48: And having received that excellent ornament, Rama began to ask the coming of that blazing thing:
entries.76.49: 'This is most wonderful and divine, endowed with an excellent form. How was it obtained by you, venerable one, and from where, and by whom was it taken?
entries.76.50: 'Out of curiosity I ask you, brahmin of great renown; for you are the highest treasury of many marvels.'
entries.76.51: As Kakutstha spoke thus, the sage said this word: 'Hear, Rama, what came to pass long ago in the age of Treta —
entries.76.52: 'the marvel I saw in this lovely region, in this forest, mighty-armed one, resting upon the matter of giving alone.'
entries.77.1: 'Long ago in the Treta age, Rama, there was a forest of wide extent, a hundred yojanas on every side, without deer and empty of birds.
entries.77.2: 'In that wilderness with no man in it I came, gentle one, wishing to enter and to perform the highest penance.
entries.77.3: 'The beauty of that forest could not be told, with its fruit and roots of sweet taste and its trees of many kinds.
entries.77.4: 'And in the midst of that forest was a lake a yojana broad, strewn with swans and karandavas and adorned with chakravakas,
entries.77.5: 'covered with lotus and lily and free of weed — a thing of the greatest wonder, of sweet taste and unmatched,
entries.77.6: 'dustless and unshaken, glorious and thronged with flocks of birds. And near that lake was a hermitage, a great marvel,
entries.77.7: 'ancient and most holy, but empty of ascetics. There I passed a night of the hot season, bull among men.
entries.77.8: 'Rising at dawn I went down to that lake; and there I saw a corpse, well-nourished and nowhere decayed,
entries.77.9: 'its limbs full and unbroken, resting there in the lake, standing with the highest beauty in that body of water, king.
entries.77.10: 'Pondering that matter, Raghava, I stayed a while upon the lake's shore, wondering, "What can this be, lord?"
entries.77.11: 'Then in a moment I saw a divine thing of wondrous seeming — a chariot most excellent, yoked with swans and swift as thought.
entries.77.12: 'And in that chariot, delight of the Raghus, a dweller in heaven; and about him, hero, a thousand apsaras with divine ornaments.
entries.77.13: 'Some sang divine songs, and others played upon instruments; some made sport, and others danced.
entries.77.14: 'And others with chowries of golden handles, bright as the moon's rays, fanned that face of his whose eyes were like white lotuses.
entries.77.15: 'Then, leaving his lion-seat as the sun leaves the peak of Meru, and coming down from the chariot before my eyes, Rama, that dweller in heaven ate that corpse, delight of the Raghus.
entries.77.16: 'Having eaten his fill of that flesh, much and very fat, that heaven-dweller went down into the lake and began to touch the water.
entries.77.17: 'Having touched the water in due form, that heaven-dweller, bull of the Raghus, began to mount that finest of chariots.
entries.77.18: 'And seeing him, who was like a god, mounting it, I spoke this word to that dweller in heaven, bull among men:
entries.77.19: '"Who are you, who are like a god? And this food is a thing condemned. Why is it eaten by you, gentle one? You should tell me.
entries.77.20: '"To whom could such a state belong, and such a food, honoured by the gods? It is a marvel, gentle one; I wish to hear it as it truly is.
entries.77.21: '"I do not think this corpse a fitting food for you."'
entries.77.22: 'Being addressed thus, lord of men, that dweller in heaven, hearing my speech spoken out of curiosity and in kindly words, told me all of it as it was.'
entries.78.1: 'Hearing my word of auspicious syllables, Rama, that heaven-dweller answered thus with joined palms, delight of the Raghus:
entries.78.2: '"Hear, brahmin, what came to pass of old in my happiness and my sorrow, and how it cannot be overpassed, since you ask me, twice-born one.
entries.78.3: '"Long ago there was a king of the Vidarbhas, my father of great renown, known in the three worlds as Sudeva, and valiant.
entries.78.4: '"To him, brahmin, two sons were born of two wives. I was known as Shveta, and the younger was Suratha.
entries.78.5: '"Then, when my father had gone to heaven, the citizens consecrated me; and there I ruled the kingdom according to dharma and with full attention.
entries.78.6: '"Thus thousands of years passed, holder of good vows, while I made the kingdom go and guarded the people according to dharma, brahmin.
entries.78.7: '"Then by some sign I knew the measure of my life, best of the twice-born; and setting the law of time in my heart, I came to the forest.
entries.78.8: '"So I entered this hard forest, empty of beast and bird, to perform penance near this fair lake,
entries.78.9: '"having consecrated my brother Suratha as lord of the earth in the kingdom. Coming to this lake, I performed penance here a long while.
entries.78.10: '"And having performed a most hard penance three thousand years in this great forest, I attained the unmatched world of Brahma.
entries.78.11: '"And being in heaven, hunger and thirst afflicted me, most generous one; and with my senses troubled I went to the Grandsire, best in the three worlds, and said:
entries.78.12: '"'Venerable one, this world of Brahma is free of hunger and thirst. Of what deed is this the ripening, that hunger and thirst follow me?
entries.78.13: '"'And what is my food, god? Tell me that, Grandsire.'
entries.78.14: '"And the Grandsire said to me: 'Your food, son of Sudeva, is your own flesh, sweet to the taste; eat that continually.
entries.78.15: '"'Your own body was made full by you while you performed that highest penance. What is not sown does not grow, Shveta, ever, great-minded one.
entries.78.16: '"'You have no satisfaction, not the least, in the forest thronged with creatures. For of old, king, when a wandering ascetic begged of you, alms were never given by you, radiant as Indra — no, not even to a guest.
entries.78.17: '"'Nothing was given by you, not the least; you served penance alone. Therefore, my child, having gone to heaven you are afflicted with hunger and thirst.
entries.78.18: '"'So do you eat that unmatched body of your own, well nourished with food; it has the taste of nectar, and by it your satisfaction shall come.
entries.78.19: '"'And when the very great sage Agastya, hard to assail, shall come to that forest, Shveta, then you shall be released from this hardship.
entries.78.20: '"'For he is able to carry across even the hosts of the gods, gentle one; how much more you, mighty-armed one, come under the power of hunger and thirst.'
entries.78.21: '"So I, having heard the resolve of the venerable god of gods, have this condemned food, my own body, best of the twice-born.
entries.78.22: '"For many thousands of years, brahmin, this has been eaten by me, and it does not come to an end, brahmarshi; and my satisfaction in it is the highest.
entries.78.23: '"Release me, who am fallen into hardship, from this hardship. There is no other refuge here but the pot-born twice-born one.
entries.78.24: '"This ornament, gentle one, is for my crossing over, best of the twice-born. Receive it — may it be well with you — and you should show me favour.
entries.78.25: '"Here is gold and wealth and garments too, twice-born one; and food to eat and food to enjoy, brahmarshi, and he gives ornaments as well.
entries.78.26: '"I give every desire and every enjoyment, bull among sages. Venerable one, you should show me favour for my crossing over."
entries.78.27: 'Hearing that speech of the heaven-dweller, full of sorrow, I took that finest ornament for his crossing over.
entries.78.28: 'And when that fair ornament had been received by me, the former human body of that royal sage was destroyed.
entries.78.29: 'And when that body was destroyed, that royal sage with the highest gladness, satisfied and rejoicing, went happily to the third heaven.
entries.78.30: 'By him, the equal of Shakra, was this divine ornament of wondrous seeming given to me on that occasion, Kakutstha.'
entries.79.1: Hearing that most wonderful speech of Agastya, Raghava, out of reverence and out of wonder, began to ask again:
entries.79.2: 'Venerable one, that dreadful forest where he performed his penance — Shveta the king of the Vidarbhas — how did it come to be without beast or bird?
entries.79.3: 'And how did that king enter that forest, empty and bereft of men, to perform his penance? I wish to hear it as it truly is.'
entries.79.4: Hearing Rama's word, full of curiosity, that one of the highest splendour began to speak:
entries.79.5: 'Long ago in the Krita age, Rama, Manu the lord was the bearer of the rod; and his son was the great Ikshvaku, the delight of his line.
entries.79.6: 'Setting that first-born son, unconquerable upon earth, in the kingdom, he said to him, "Be the founder of the royal lines upon the earth."
entries.79.7: 'And so it was promised by the son to his father, Raghava; and then Manu, well pleased, said to his son:
entries.79.8: '"I am pleased, most generous one; you shall be the founder, and there is no doubt of it. Guard the people with the rod, and do not use the rod without cause.
entries.79.9: '"The rod which falls upon offending men — that rod, loosed according to the ordinance, leads a king to heaven.
entries.79.10: '"Therefore be diligent in the rod, mighty-armed one, my son. There shall be the highest dharma for you in the world as you do it."
entries.79.11: 'Having thus instructed his son at length and with a composed mind, Manu went gladly to the third heaven, to the eternal world of Brahma.
entries.79.12: 'When he had gone to the third heaven, Ikshvaku of measureless splendour became given to the thought, "How shall I beget sons?"
entries.79.13: 'And by works of many kinds that soul of dharma, the son of Manu, begot a hundred sons like the sons of the gods.
entries.79.14: 'And the youngest of them all, dear one, delight of the Raghus, was dull and untaught, and did not serve his elders.
entries.79.15: 'And his father made his name Danda, "the Rod," for that one of little wit: "The falling of the rod upon his body will surely come."
entries.79.16: 'Not seeing any dreadful region for his son, Raghava, he gave him a kingdom between the Vindhya and the Shaivala, subduer of foes.
entries.79.17: 'And there Danda became king upon a lovely mountain slope, and he settled a matchless and unequalled city, Rama.
entries.79.18: 'And he made the name of the city Madhumanta, lord; and he chose as household priest Ushanas of good vows.
entries.79.19: 'Thus that king with his household priest made that kingdom go, thronged with glad men, as the bull among gods rules his own.
entries.79.20: 'Then that king, the son of the lord of men, together with that Ushanas, ruled a very great kingdom, that great soul, as Shakra in heaven with Ushanas beside him.'
entries.80.1: Having told this to Rama, the great sage born of the pot began another word within that very tale:
entries.80.2: 'Then that Danda, Kakutstha, self-controlled, made a kingdom there without a thorn in it for many thousands of years.
entries.80.3: 'Then at some time the king came to the lovely hermitage of Bhargava in the pleasant month of Chaitra.
entries.80.4: 'And there Danda saw the daughter of Bhargava, unmatched in beauty upon the earth, wandering in a corner of the wood, one beyond compare.
entries.80.5: 'Seeing her, that most evil-witted one, stricken by the arrows of Ananga, came to that maiden greatly troubled and said this word:
entries.80.6: '"From where are you, fair-hipped one, and whose daughter are you, auspicious one? I am afflicted by Ananga, and I go to you, fair-faced one."
entries.80.7: 'To him speaking so, bewildered with delusion and full of desire, the daughter of Bhargava answered the king with this word of conciliation:
entries.80.8: '"Know me for the daughter of the god Bhargava, whose deeds are done without effort — Araja by name, lord of kings, the elder, dwelling in the hermitage.
entries.80.9: '"Do not touch me by force, king; I am a maiden and in my father's power. My father, lord of kings, is your teacher and you the disciple of that great soul; and being angered, that one of great penance would give you a very great calamity.
entries.80.10: '"Or if anything else is to be done by me according to the good path that dharma sees, then ask my father of great splendour, best of men.
entries.80.11: '"Otherwise a fruit dreadfully appointed would be yours; for that father of mine in his wrath could burn up even the three worlds.
entries.80.12: '"And my father, if you ask him, will give me to you, one of blameless limbs."
entries.80.13: 'To Araja speaking thus, Danda, being fallen under the power of desire, answered, mad with intoxication, setting his joined palms upon his head:
entries.80.14: '"Show me favour, fair-hipped one; you should not spend the hour. For my life is being torn apart for your sake, fair-faced one.
entries.80.15: '"Having obtained you, let my death come, or a dreadful curse. Serve me who am your servant, timid one — one who serves you and is greatly distressed."
entries.80.16: 'Having spoken thus, that strong one seized that maiden by force with his two arms and, as she struggled, went about the act of union as he pleased.
entries.80.17: 'Having done this most dreadful and cruel deed, Danda went swiftly to that unmatched city Madhumanta.
entries.80.18: 'And Araja too, weeping, not far from the hermitage, greatly terrified, waited for her father who was like a god.'
entries.81.1: 'In a moment that divine sage of measureless splendour, hearing of it, turned back to his own hermitage, surrounded by his disciples and afflicted with hunger.
entries.81.2: 'And he saw Araja wretched and overwhelmed with defilement, like moonlight seized by a planet, giving no light at dawn.
entries.81.3: 'And anger arose in him, being afflicted with hunger above all; and as though burning up the three worlds he said this to his disciples:
entries.81.4: '"Look upon the calamity of the perverse Danda, whose soul is unconquered — a calamity dreadful to look upon, wrathful as a tongue of fire.
entries.81.5: '"Destruction has come upon that evil-minded one, that evil soul with his followers, who wished to touch the blazing flame of the eater of oblations.
entries.81.6: '"Since he has done a sin of such a kind, joined with dreadful things, therefore that dull-witted one shall obtain the fruit of his sinful deed.
entries.81.7: '"Within seven nights that king with his servants and forces and mounts, that evil-minded one of sinful conduct, shall meet his destruction.
entries.81.8: '"And a hundred yojanas about, the realm of that evil-minded one shall be burnt by the chastiser of Paka with a great rain of dust.
entries.81.9: '"And all the beings that are here, moving and unmoving, shall come to dissolution on every side by that great rain of dust.
entries.81.10: '"As far as Danda's realm extends, so far shall there be, covering all that stands high, a rain of dust past sight, for seven nights."
entries.81.11: 'Having spoken thus, his eyes red with anger, he told the people who dwelt in that hermitage to take their station at the borders of the country.
entries.81.12: 'Hearing Ushanas' word, that people who dwelt in the hermitage went out from that realm and made their dwelling beyond it.
entries.81.13: 'And having so spoken to the people of the sages, he said this to Araja: "Dwell here in this very hermitage, dull-witted one, with full attention.
entries.81.14: '"This lake, a yojana in compass and of shining beauty — Araja, live free of fever upon it, and await here the appointed time.
entries.81.15: '"And those creatures who shall come to dwell near you that night shall always be unslayable by that rain of dust."
entries.81.16: 'Hearing the brahmarshi's command, that daughter of Bhargava, Araja, said 'So be it' to her father Bhargava, being deeply grieved; and having spoken thus, Bhargava had his dwelling made elsewhere.
entries.81.17: 'And that kingdom of the lord of men, with his servants and forces and mounts, was reduced to ashes within seven days, as the speaker of Brahman had said.
entries.81.18: 'So that realm of Danda between the Vindhya and the Shaivala, king, was cursed by that brahmarshi when unrighteousness was joined with the deed.
entries.81.19: 'And from that time, Kakutstha, it is called the Dandaka forest. And because ascetics settled here, it became Janasthana.
entries.81.20: 'All this has been told you which you asked of me, Raghava. It is time to attend upon the twilight, hero, for the hour is passing.
entries.81.21: 'These great sages all about with their full jars, their water-rites performed, tiger among men, are worshipping the sun.
entries.81.22: 'The sun has set, Rama, and by those best knowers of Brahman gathered together the Vedic recitation has been performed. Go and touch the water.'
entries.82.1: Understanding the sage's word, Rama went to that holy lake frequented by the hosts of apsaras, to worship the twilight.
entries.82.2: Having touched the water there and attended upon the western twilight, Rama entered the hermitage of the great-souled pot-born.
entries.82.3: And Agastya prepared for his eating roots and herbs of many virtues, and rice and other pure things.
entries.82.4: And that best of men, having eaten that food which was like nectar, pleased and wholly satisfied, sat through that night.
entries.82.5: Rising at dawn and performing the daily rites, that subduer of foes, best of the Raghus, came to the sage to take his leave.
entries.82.6: Saluting him, Rama said to the great sage born of the pot: 'I ask leave to go to my own city; you should give me leave.
entries.82.7: 'I am blessed and I am favoured by the sight of that great soul; and I shall come again to see you, for my own purifying.'
entries.82.8: As Kakutstha spoke that word of wondrous seeming, that treasury of penance whose eye is dharma said with the highest pleasure:
entries.82.9: 'This word of yours is most wonderful and of auspicious syllables, Rama. You yourself are the purifier of all beings, delight of the Raghus.
entries.82.10: 'Whoever look upon you even for a moment, Rama, are purified and become dwellers in heaven, and are to be honoured by all the gods.
entries.82.11: 'And those creatures upon the earth who look upon you with a dreadful eye are slain by the rod of Yama and go at once to hell.
entries.82.12: 'Such are you, best of the Raghus, the purifier of all who bear bodies; and even those who tell of you upon the earth shall come to perfection, Raghava.
entries.82.13: 'Go by a road that is safe and unhindered and free of fear from any quarter. Rule the kingdom in dharma; for you are the refuge of the world.'
entries.82.14: Being addressed thus by the sage, that wise king with joined palms and in restraint saluted that sage rich in merit.
entries.82.15: Saluting that best of sages and all those treasuries of penance, he mounted without haste the Pushpaka adorned with gold.
entries.82.16: And as he went the hosts of sages honoured him on every side with their blessings — him who was like Mahendra — as the immortals honour the thousand-eyed one.
entries.82.17: And Rama, at his ease in the Pushpaka adorned with gold, was seen as the moon is seen standing near a cloud at the coming of the rains.
entries.82.18: Then at midday, being honoured here and there, Kakutstha came to Ayodhya and came down at the middle court.
entries.82.19: Then dismissing that lovely Pushpaka which goes where it is wished, that lord dismissed it with 'Go, and may it be well with you.'
entries.82.20: And Rama said this word to the doorkeeper stationed at the inner court: 'Go, you two of swift step, to Lakshmana and to Bharata; announce my coming and call them, and do not delay.'
entries.83.1: Hearing that speech of Rama, whose deeds are done without effort, the doorkeeper called the princes and announced them to Raghava.
entries.83.2: Seeing his dear ones Bharata and Lakshmana arrived, Rama embraced them and said this word:
entries.83.3: 'The unmatched business of the brahmin has been done by me as it truly should be. Now I wish to make yet again a bridge of dharma, you two Raghavas.
entries.83.4: 'A bridge of dharma is held by me to be imperishable and unfailing; for this is what accomplishes dharma and destroys all sin.
entries.83.5: 'With you two, who are my very self, I wish to sacrifice with the unmatched Rajasuya; for there dharma is everlasting.
entries.83.6: 'For Mitra, the destroyer of foes, having sacrificed with the Rajasuya, with a well-offered and excellent sacrifice, came to the station of Varuna.
entries.83.7: 'And Soma, the knower of dharma, having sacrificed with the Rajasuya according to dharma, attained an everlasting place of fame in all the worlds.
entries.83.8: 'Let what is best on this day be considered with me. You should both take pains to do what is beneficial and joined with what is to come.'
entries.83.9: Hearing that word of Raghava, Bharata, skilled in speech, with joined palms said this word:
entries.83.10: 'In you is the highest dharma, good one, and in you the whole earth is established, mighty-armed one, and glory too, one of measureless valour.
entries.83.11: 'And all the guardians of the earth look upon you, that great soul, as the immortals look upon Prajapati and as we look upon the lord of the world.
entries.83.12: 'And sons look upon you as upon a father, king of great strength; you are the refuge of the earth and of all living creatures too, Raghava.
entries.83.13: 'How then will you undertake a sacrifice of such a kind, king, in which the destruction of the royal lines upon the earth is seen?
entries.83.14: 'And of all those men upon the earth, king, who have come to manhood, there will be a destruction there arising out of the anger of all.
entries.83.15: 'So you, tiger among men, of unmatched valour and virtue, should not destroy the earth; for it stands already under your sway.'
entries.83.16: Hearing that word of Bharata's, full of nectar, Rama of true valour felt a joy beyond compare.
entries.83.17: And he said an auspicious word that increased the joy of Kaikeyi: 'I am pleased and wholly satisfied today with your speech, sinless one.
entries.83.18: 'This word of yours, unweak and settled in dharma, has been uttered, tiger among men, for the guarding of the earth.
entries.83.19: 'From the Rajasuya, that best of sacrifices which was my intention, I turn back, knower of dharma, at your well-spoken word.
entries.83.20: 'A deed that brings affliction upon the world should not be done by the discerning. Even the auspicious word of the young should be taken, elder brother of Lakshmana. Therefore I hear your word, well and fitly spoken, great-minded one.'
entries.84.1: When Rama and the great-souled Bharata had spoken thus, Lakshmana said an auspicious word to the delight of the Raghus:
entries.84.2: 'The horse-sacrifice is a great rite and the purifier of all sins; let it please you, delight of the Raghus, for it is the purifier and hard to assail.
entries.84.3: 'It is heard that it happened of old to the great-souled Vasava: Shakra, being wrapped about with the guilt of a brahmin's death, was purified by the horse-sacrifice.
entries.84.4: 'Long ago, mighty-armed one, at the meeting of gods and asuras, there was a great son of Diti named Vritra, honoured by the world.
entries.84.5: 'He was a hundred yojanas broad and three times as tall; and with affection and out of love he looked upon the three worlds on every side.
entries.84.6: 'A knower of dharma, grateful, and settled in understanding, he ruled the flourishing earth in dharma and with full attention.
entries.84.7: 'While he ruled, the earth yielded every desire, and there were roots and fruits full of savour and abundance.
entries.84.8: 'The earth ripened without ploughing and was full of wealth for that great soul; and he enjoyed such a kingdom, flourishing and wonderful to see.
entries.84.9: 'Then this thought arose in him: "Let me perform an unmatched penance; for penance is the highest good, and other happiness is a delusion."
entries.84.10: 'And having set his eldest son among the citizens as lord of Madhura, he undertook a fierce penance, scorching all the deities.
entries.84.11: 'And as Vritra performed that penance, Vasava, greatly afflicted, came to Vishnu and said this word:
entries.84.12: '"Mighty-armed one, the worlds have been conquered by Vritra as he practises penance. He is strong and a soul of dharma, and I shall not be able to master him.
entries.84.13: '"If that lord of asuras should stand yet again in penance, then so long as the worlds endure, so long shall they follow his will.
entries.84.14: '"And you look on at that most generous one of great strength. For Vritra would not last a moment if you were angered, lord of the gods.
entries.84.15: '"For from the time he came into a joining of affection with you, Vishnu, from that time he has obtained the lordship of the worlds.
entries.84.16: '"So do you show favour to the worlds, with full attention. For by what you do, the whole world would be quieted and free of ill.
entries.84.17: '"All these dwellers in heaven look to you, Vishnu; give them your help by the great slaying of Vritra.
entries.84.18: '"For by you help has always been given to these great souls. This is not to be borne by others; you are the refuge of those who have none."'
entries.85.1: Hearing that word of Lakshmana, that destroyer of foes said, 'Tell the slaying of Vritra without leaving anything out, holder of good vows.'
entries.85.2: Being addressed thus by Raghava, that increaser of Sumitra's joy, of good vows, told that divine tale once again.
entries.85.3: 'Hearing the word of the thousand-eyed one and of all the dwellers in heaven, Vishnu said this to all the gods with Indra at their head:
entries.85.4: '"I am bound in friendship of old with that great soul Vritra; and therefore, for your pleasure, I do not slay that great asura.
entries.85.5: '"Yet the highest happiness must certainly be brought about for you. Therefore I shall tell you a means by which Vritra may be slain.
entries.85.6: '"I shall make myself threefold, best of the gods; and by that the thousand-eyed one shall slay Vritra, and there is no doubt.
entries.85.7: '"Let one portion go to Vasava, the second to the thunderbolt itself, and the third to the earth; then Shakra shall slay Vritra."
entries.85.8: 'As the lord of the gods spoke so, the gods said this word: "So it is, and there is no doubt, as you say, slayer of daityas.
entries.85.9: '"May it be well with you; we shall go, desiring the slaying of the asura Vritra. Enter into Vasava with your own splendour, most generous one."
entries.85.10: 'Then all those great souls with the thousand-eyed one at their head went to that forest where the great asura Vritra was.
entries.85.11: 'They saw that best of asuras made of splendour, performing his penance, as though drinking up the three worlds and burning up the sky.
entries.85.12: 'And at the mere sight of that best of asuras the gods were seized with terror: "How shall we slay him, and how shall there be no defeat for us?"
entries.85.13: 'And as they were thinking so, the thousand-eyed Purandara took the thunderbolt in both his hands and hurled it at Vritra's head.
entries.85.14: 'By that head of Vritra as it fell, dreadful as the fire of Kala and blazing with a great flame, the world was seized with terror.
entries.85.15: 'And the lord of the wise, thinking that the slaying of that Vritra was a thing that should not have been, that greatly renowned one went swiftly to the end of the world.
entries.85.16: 'And the guilt of the brahmin's death followed after Indra as he went, and fell upon his limbs; and sorrow entered Indra.
entries.85.17: 'With their enemies slain but their Indra lost, the gods with Agni at their head honoured Vishnu, the lord of the three worlds, again and again:
entries.85.18: '"You are the refuge, supreme lord, the first-born and the father of the world; for the guarding of all beings you came to the state of Vishnu.
entries.85.19: '"This Vritra was slain by you, and now the guilt of a brahmin's death afflicts Vasava, tiger among the gods. Appoint a release from it."
entries.85.20: 'Hearing that word of theirs, Vishnu said to the gods: "Let Shakra sacrifice to me alone, and I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt.
entries.85.21: '"Having sacrificed to me with the holy horse-sacrifice, the chastiser of Paka shall come again to the lordship of the gods, with nothing to fear from any quarter."
entries.85.22: 'Having so appointed that word to the gods, which was like nectar, Vishnu the lord of the gods went to the third heaven, being praised.'
entries.86.1: Then, having told the whole slaying of Vritra without leaving anything out, that best of men, Lakshmana, began the remainder of the tale.
entries.86.2: 'When Vritra of great valour, the terror of the gods, had been slain, Shakra, wrapped about with the guilt of a brahmin's death, did not recover his senses, though he was Vritra's slayer.
entries.86.3: 'Taking refuge at the end of the worlds, his senses lost and without consciousness, he dwelt there some time, writhing as it were like a serpent.
entries.86.4: 'And when the thousand-eyed one was thus lost, the world became troubled, and the earth looked ruined, without moisture and with its woods dried up.
entries.86.5: 'And all the pools and rivers were without their streams; and there was an agitation of living creatures brought about by the failure of rain.
entries.86.6: 'And as this world was wasting away, the gods, troubled in mind, brought about that sacrifice which had been spoken of before by Vishnu.
entries.86.7: 'Then all the hosts of gods, with their teachers and with the sages, came to that place where Indra was, bewildered with fear.
entries.86.8: 'And seeing the thousand-eyed one wrapped about with the guilt of a brahmin's death, they set that lord of the gods before them and began the horse-sacrifice.
entries.86.9: 'Then that very great horse-sacrifice of the great-souled Mahendra grew, for the purifying of the guilt of a brahmin's death, lord of men.
entries.86.10: 'Then, when the sacrifice was ended, the guilt of a brahmin's death came to that great soul and said this word: "Where will you appoint a place for me?"
entries.86.11: 'Then the gods, being satisfied and filled with pleasure, said to her: "Divide yourself in four by your own self, one hard to assail."
entries.86.12: 'Hearing the speech of those great-souled gods, the guilt of a brahmin's death, being hard to dwell with, chose a place elsewhere than in their presence:
entries.86.13: '"With one portion I shall dwell in the rivers when they are in full flood, for the four months of the rains, the destroyer of pride and the withholder of water.
entries.86.14: '"And with one portion I shall dwell always upon the earth at all times, and there is no doubt; I tell you this in truth.
entries.86.15: '"And this third portion of mine shall dwell for three nights in women in the bloom of youth when they are full of pride, being the destroyer of pride.
entries.86.16: '"And those who slay brahmins that are undefiled, out of falsehood — those I shall take refuge in with the fourth portion, bulls among the gods."
entries.86.17: 'Then the gods answered her: "As you say, hard one to dwell with, so let all of it be. Accomplish what you desire."
entries.86.18: 'Then the gods, filled with pleasure, saluted the thousand-eyed one; and Vasava became free of fever and purified in soul.
entries.86.19: 'And the whole world was quieted when the thousand-eyed one was established again; and Shakra then honoured that sacrifice of wondrous seeming.
entries.86.20: 'Such is the grace of the horse-sacrifice, delight of the Raghus. Sacrifice, greatly blessed one, with the horse-sacrifice, lord of earth.'
entries.86.21: Hearing that excellent and most delightful word of Lakshmana, that great-souled king, whose valour and might were the equal of Indra's, came to the highest satisfaction with a glad heart.
entries.87.1: Hearing that word spoken by Lakshmana, Raghava of great splendour, skilled in speech, answered laughing:
entries.87.2: 'It is even so, best of men, as you say, Lakshmana — the slaying of Vritra without omission, and what is the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
entries.87.3: 'For it is heard, gentle one, that long ago Prajapati Kardama had a son, the glorious lord of Bahli, named Ila, of great spirit.
entries.87.4: 'That king, most righteous, brought the whole earth under his sway and guarded the kingdom as a father guards a son, tiger among men.
entries.87.5: 'By the gods most generous and by the sons of Diti of great wealth, by nagas and rakshasas and gandharvas and by yakshas of great soul,
entries.87.6: 'he was honoured continually, gentle one, by those afflicted with fear, delight of the Raghus; and the three worlds feared that great soul when he was angered.
entries.87.7: 'Such was that king, established in dharma and in valour, most generous in understanding, that greatly renowned lord of the Bahlikas.
entries.87.8: 'And that mighty-armed one went hunting in a lovely wood, in the delightful month of Chaitra, with his servants and forces and mounts.
entries.87.9: 'And the king slew deer in that forest by hundreds and thousands; and even by that slaying there came no satisfaction to that great-souled king.
entries.87.10: 'Slaying a myriad of deer of many kinds, that great soul came to that region where Mahasena was born.
entries.87.11: 'In that region the lord of the gods, Hara, hard to assail, was giving delight to the daughter of the mountain king, together with all his attendants.
entries.87.12: 'The lord of Uma, whose banner is the bull, having made himself into the form of a woman, wishing to do what pleased the goddess, was there upon that mountain torrent.
entries.87.13: 'And whatever creatures were there in that corner of the wood that were called male, and the trees that bore male names, they all became female then.
entries.87.14: 'And whatever there was, all of it came to bear a woman's name. And in this interval that king Ila, the son of Kardama, slaying deer by thousands, came to that region.
entries.87.15: 'And he saw all made female, with the beasts and deer and birds, and himself made female too, with his followers, delight of the Raghus.
entries.87.16: 'And there was a great sorrow to him, seeing himself come to such a state; and knowing that deed of Uma's lord, he came to terror.
entries.87.17: 'Then that king with his servants and forces and mounts went for refuge to the great-souled god of the dark throat and the matted hair.
entries.87.18: 'Then Maheshvara, the giver of boons, laughing with the goddess, himself the giver of boons, said this word to the son of Prajapati:
entries.87.19: '"Rise, rise, royal sage, son of Kardama of great strength. Choose a boon, gentle one of good vows — anything but manhood."
entries.87.20: 'Then that king, afflicted with sorrow and refused by that great soul, being made a woman, would not take another boon from that best of the gods.
entries.87.21: 'Then with a great grief the king bowed to the daughter of the mountain king, to the goddess Uma, with his whole inmost soul:
entries.87.22: '"You are the mistress of boons and the giver of boons, and the lovely lady of the worlds. Goddess whose sight is not in vain, look upon me with a gentle eye."
entries.87.23: 'Knowing what was in the heart of that royal sage, the goddess honoured of Rudra answered in his presence with an auspicious word:
entries.87.24: '"The god is the giver of half the boon, and I of the other half. Therefore take you half, of woman and of man, as much as you wish."
entries.87.25: 'Hearing that most wonderful and unmatched boon of the goddess, the king, with a heart made most glad, then said this word:
entries.87.26: '"If you are pleased with me, goddess unmatched in beauty upon the earth, let me pass a month in womanhood and be a man again the next month."
entries.87.27: 'Knowing what he desired, the goddess of the most lovely face answered with an auspicious word: "So shall it be.
entries.87.28: '"King, when you are a man you shall not remember your state as a woman; and when you are a woman for the other month you shall not remember your manhood."
entries.87.29: 'Thus that king, the son of Kardama, was a man for a month; and for one month he was Ila, a woman, the loveliest in the three worlds.'
entries.88.1: Hearing that tale concerning Ila, told by Rama, Lakshmana and Bharata were filled with the highest wonder.
entries.88.2: And those two, with joined palms, asked Rama again for the full account of that state of the great-souled king:
entries.88.3: 'How did that king, being made a woman, live in that hard condition? And when he was made a man, what manner of life did he live?'
entries.88.4: Hearing that speech of theirs, full of curiosity, Kakutstha told what had come to that king.
entries.88.5: 'In that very first month, being made a woman, that loveliest in the world, surrounded by those women who had before been his followers,
entries.88.6: 'entered that forest swiftly and sported there, that loveliest in the world with eyes like lotus petals, going on foot through a place strewn with trees and thickets and creepers.
entries.88.7: 'And having left all her mounts about her on every side, Ila took her pleasure in a hollow of that mountain's expanse.
entries.88.8: 'And in that corner of the wood, not far from the mountain, there was a lake of shining beauty, thronged with flocks of birds of many kinds.
entries.88.9: 'And there Ila saw Budha, the son of Soma, blazing with his own body like the full moon risen,
entries.88.10: 'performing a fierce penance in the midst of the water, hard to approach, a maker of fame, a doer of what is desired, and established in compassion.
entries.88.11: 'And she in wonder troubled the whole of that body of water, together with those who went with her, who had before been men and were now women, delight of the Raghus.
entries.88.12: 'And Budha, at the mere sight of her, fell under the power of Kama's arrows; he could not then find himself, and moved about in the water.
entries.88.13: 'And gazing upon Ila, auspicious and beyond the three worlds, he passed into thought: "Who then is this, who is more than a goddess?
entries.88.14: '"Not among the goddesses, nor among the nagini, nor among the asura women or the apsaras, have I seen any before adorned with such beauty as this.
entries.88.15: '"She would be a match for me, if she is not another's already." And settling upon that thought, he came from the water to the shore.
entries.88.16: 'And coming to his hermitage, that soul of dharma called those best of women; and they came and did him honour.
entries.88.17: 'And that soul of dharma asked them: "Whose is this loveliest in the world? And why has she come? Tell me it all, and do not delay."
entries.88.18: 'Hearing that auspicious word of his, sweet and of sweet syllables, all those women answered in a sweet voice:
entries.88.19: '"This fair-hipped one is always in lordship over us. She is without a husband, and she moves in the depths of the woods with us."
entries.88.20: 'Hearing that word of those women, whose sense was not made plain, that twice-born one turned over in his mind the holy science of recollection.
entries.88.21: 'And knowing the whole matter of that king, and how it had come about, that bull among sages said to all those women:
entries.88.22: '"You shall dwell here upon the mountain slope, having become kimpurushis. Let a dwelling be made for you upon this mountain at once.
entries.88.23: '"You shall live always upon roots and leaves and fruit; and as women you shall obtain husbands called kimpurushas."
entries.88.24: 'Hearing that word of Soma's son and being made kimpurushis, those many brides then took their dwelling upon that mountain.'
entries.89.1: Hearing the origin of the kimpurushas, Lakshmana and Bharata both said 'It is a marvel' to Rama, the lord of men.
entries.89.2: Then that greatly renowned Rama, a soul of dharma, told that tale of Prajapati's son yet again.
entries.89.3: 'Seeing all those kinnaris fled away, that best of sages said, as it were laughing, to that woman endowed with beauty:
entries.89.4: '"I am the dearly loved son of Soma, one of the loveliest face. Serve me, fair-hipped one, with devotion and with a tender eye."
entries.89.5: 'Hearing that word of his in that place, empty and bereft of her own people, Ila of shining beauty answered him of great seizing power:
entries.89.6: '"I go where I wish, gentle one, and I am under your will. Command me, son of Soma; do as you desire."
entries.89.7: 'Hearing that word of hers, of wondrous seeming, he came to gladness; and that lover, the son of the moon, took his pleasure with her.
entries.89.8: 'And the month of Madhava passed for Budha as he took his pleasure exceedingly with that Ila of the lovely face — it passed for that lover as though it were a moment.
entries.89.9: 'Then when the month was full, that glorious son of Prajapati, whose face was like the full moon, awoke upon his couch.
entries.89.10: 'And he saw there the son of Soma performing penance in the body of water, with his arms upraised and without support; and the king said to him:
entries.89.11: '"Venerable one, I entered this hard mountain with my followers, and I do not see that army of mine. Where have my people gone?"
entries.89.12: 'Hearing that speech of the royal sage, whose memory was lost, he answered with an auspicious word, comforting him in the highest tones:
entries.89.13: '"Your servants were struck down by a great rain of stones; and you slept in this hermitage, afflicted by the terror of wind and rain.
entries.89.14: '"Take comfort; may it be well with you. Free of fear and free of fever, hero, live here at your ease, eating fruit and root."
entries.89.15: 'That king of great mind, being comforted by that word, then said a word, deeply wretched at the loss of his servants:
entries.89.16: '"I shall give up my own kingdom; without my servants I shall not live a moment, brahmin. You should give me leave.
entries.89.17: '"I have a son devoted to dharma, brahmin, my eldest, of great renown, known as Shashabindu; he shall take my kingdom.
entries.89.18: '"For I shall not be able, having left my servants and their wives who were joined with happiness, to answer even a single word that is not auspicious, one of great splendour."
entries.89.19: 'As that lord of kings was speaking so, Budha, in the greatest wonder, said with conciliation first: "Let a dwelling here please you.
entries.89.20: '"You should not grieve, son of Kardama of great strength. When you have dwelt here a year, I shall bring about your welfare."
entries.89.21: 'Hearing that word of Budha, whose deeds are done without effort, he set his mind upon dwelling there, as the speaker of Brahman had said.
entries.89.22: 'For a month he became a woman then and took his pleasure without ceasing in gladness; and for a month, in the state of a man, he set his mind upon dharma.
entries.89.23: 'Then in the ninth month that fair-hipped Ila bore a son to the son of Soma — Pururavas, endowed with might.
entries.89.24: 'And as soon as he was born, that fair-hipped one placed the child in his father's hands — Ila placed in Budha's hands that mighty son of like complexion.
entries.89.25: 'And Budha, self-possessed, gave him delight for the space of a year, when he was in the state of a man, with tales joined with dharma.'
entries.90.1: As Rama told that wondrous birth of his, Lakshmana said again, and the greatly renowned Bharata:
entries.90.2: 'That Ila, having dwelt a year with the son of Soma, what did she do then, best of men? You should tell us truly.'
entries.90.3: Hearing the sweetness of that word of theirs as they asked, Rama told once more this tale of Prajapati's son.
entries.90.4: 'When that hero had come to manhood, Budha of the highest understanding, of great renown, called Samvarta, that most generous one,
entries.90.5: 'and Chyavana the son of Bhrigu, and the sage Arishtanemi, Pramodana and Modakara, and then the sage Durvasa.
entries.90.6: 'Having gathered all these, that knower of speech and seer of the truth said to all those friends, gathered with steadiness and full attention:
entries.90.7: '"This mighty-armed king is Ila, the son of Kardama. Know him as he truly is, and let what is best be appointed here."
entries.90.8: 'And as they were speaking thus, Kardama of great splendour came to that hermitage with great-souled twice-born ones.
entries.90.9: 'And Pulastya and Kratu, and Vashatkara likewise, and Omkara of great splendour, came to that hermitage.
entries.90.10: 'And all of them, glad in mind at meeting one another, wishing well to the lord of Bahli, spoke their words each in turn.
entries.90.11: 'And Kardama said a word of the highest good for his son's sake: "Twice-born ones, hear my word, which is the best for this king.
entries.90.12: '"I see no other remedy but the bull-bannered one; there is no sacrifice higher than the horse-sacrifice, and it is dear to that great soul. Therefore let us all sacrifice with that rite, hard to attain, for the king's sake."
entries.90.13: 'Being addressed thus by Kardama, all those bulls among the twice-born were pleased with that sacrifice for the propitiating of Rudra.
entries.90.14: 'And the disciple of the royal sage Samvarta, the conqueror of his enemies' cities, renowned as Marutta, brought that sacrifice about.
entries.90.15: 'Then there was a great sacrifice near Budha's hermitage; and Rudra of great renown came to the highest satisfaction.
entries.90.16: 'Then, when the sacrifice was ended, being pleased with the highest joy, the lord of Uma said to all the twice-born in Ila's presence:
entries.90.17: '"I am pleased with the horse-sacrifice and with your devotion, best of the twice-born. What auspicious thing shall I do that would please this lord of Bahli?"
entries.90.18: 'As the lord of the gods spoke so, those twice-born ones with full attention won the favour of the lord of the gods, that Ila might become a man.
entries.90.19: 'Then the great god, being pleased, gave manhood again to Ila; and that one of very great splendour, having given it, vanished away.
entries.90.20: 'When the horse-sacrifice was ended, Hara passed out of sight; and all those far-seeing twice-born ones went as they had come.
entries.90.21: 'And the king, leaving Bahli, settled in the middle country a city unmatched and a maker of fame, Pratishthana.
entries.90.22: 'And the royal sage Shashabindu, conqueror of his enemies' cities, held Bahli; and King Ila, the mighty son of Prajapati, held Pratishthana.
entries.90.23: 'And in due time Ila attained the unmatched world of Brahma; and King Pururavas, the son of Ila, obtained Pratishthana.
entries.90.24: 'Such is the power of the horse-sacrifice, you two bulls among men — that one made a woman obtained manhood, and whatever else besides is hard to obtain.'
entries.91.1: Having told this to his two brothers, Kakutstha of measureless splendour said again to Lakshmana this word joined with dharma:
entries.91.2: 'Vasishtha and Vamadeva, Jabali and Kashyapa, and all the foremost twice-born who set the horse-sacrifice before them —
entries.91.3: 'having gathered all these and taken counsel, Lakshmana, I shall release with full attention a horse endowed with the marks.'
entries.91.4: Hearing that word spoken by Raghava, he of swift valour called all the twice-born and showed them to Raghava.
entries.91.5: And seeing that Raghava, hard to assail and like a god, making salutation at their feet, they honoured him with their blessings.
entries.91.6: Then that greatly renowned Raghava, with joined palms, declared to those best of the twice-born his intention concerning the horse-sacrifice.
entries.91.7: And hearing that of Rama, all those twice-born saluted the bull-bannered one and honoured the horse-sacrifice in every way.
entries.91.8: And hearing that word of those chief among the twice-born, of wondrous seeming and resting upon the horse-sacrifice, he was then greatly pleased.
entries.91.9: Knowing that work of theirs, Rama said to Lakshmana: 'Send messengers swiftly to the great-souled Sugriva,
entries.91.10: 'that he may come with many great monkeys and dwellers in the woods — may it be well with you — to share in this great festival.
entries.91.11: 'And let Vibhishana of unmatched valour come to this great sacrifice of the horse, surrounded by many rakshasas who go where they wish.
entries.91.12: 'And let those greatly blessed kings who wish to do what pleases me come swiftly with their followers to see this unmatched sacrifice.
entries.91.13: 'And those twice-born ones settled in dharma who have gone to other lands — invite them all, Lakshmana, to the horse-sacrifice.
entries.91.14: 'And let the sages rich in penance be called, mighty-armed one; and all the twice-born gone to other lands, with their wives, and likewise the players of cymbals and the actors and dancers.
entries.91.15: 'And let a very great sacrificial enclosure be ordered, mighty-armed one, in the Naimisha wood upon the Gomati; for that place is holy and unmatched.
entries.91.16: 'And let the rites of appeasement be set going on every side, mighty-armed one.
entries.91.17: 'And by hundreds those knowers of dharma, having shared in that best and unmatched of rites, that great sacrifice at Naimisha, delight of the Raghus —
entries.91.18: 'satisfied and nourished and honoured according to the ordinance — shall come to gladness, knower of dharma. Let the people be invited swiftly.
entries.91.19: 'Let a hundred thousand cartloads of fine rice go before, and ten thousand of sesame and mung beans, one of great strength;
entries.91.20: 'and of chickpeas and horse-gram and black gram and salt, and oil and fragrances answering to them, and all of it in brief.
entries.91.21: 'And crores of gold and hundreds more of silver — let Bharata set these before him and go ahead with full attention.
entries.91.22: 'And in between let there be rows of shops, and all the actors and dancers, and cooks, and many women always in the bloom of youth.
entries.91.23: 'Let these and the armies go before with Bharata, and the men of the guilds and those grown strong and the twice-born, with full attention.
entries.91.24: 'The workmen and the carpenters, the treasurers and the guildsmen; and all my mothers and the inner apartments of the princes,
entries.91.25: 'and my golden wife for the consecration, and those who know the rites. Let the greatly renowned Bharata set all these before him and go ahead.'
entries.91.26: And that best of men of great strength ordered costly lodgings for those kings of great might, with their followers.
entries.92.1: Having sent all of this forward swiftly and without omission, the elder brother of Bharata released a black-marked horse endowed with the signs.
entries.92.2: And having appointed Lakshmana with the officiants to the charge of the horse, Kakutstha went with his army to Naimisha.
entries.92.3: And seeing that most wonderful sacrificial enclosure, that mighty-armed and glorious one came to a joy beyond compare and said this word.
entries.92.4: And as he dwelt at Naimisha all the lords of men brought presents, and Rama honoured them in return.
entries.92.5: And that best of men, of great mind, ordered costly lodgings for those great-souled kings with their followers.
entries.92.6: And Bharata with Shatrughna swiftly gave food and drink and garments to those great souls and their followers.
entries.92.7: And the great-souled monkeys with Sugriva, all humbly, performed the serving of food to the brahmins.
entries.92.8: And Vibhishana, surrounded by many rakshasas wearing garlands, did honour to the great-souled sages of fierce penance.
entries.92.9: Thus the horse-sacrifice went forward, well appointed; and the course of the horse went on, guarded by Lakshmana. Such was that best and highest sacrifice of that lion among kings.
entries.92.10: And no other word was heard there in that great one's horse-sacrifice than 'Give at your pleasure, without hesitation, until the askers are satisfied.'
entries.92.11: And so long, all things were given in the midst of that great one's rite — sweets of many kinds made with molasses and with sugar.
entries.92.12: Before a word could come from the lips of those who asked, it was seen already given by the monkeys and the rakshasas.
entries.92.13: And there was none there soiled or wretched or wasted, in that best of sacrifices of the king, thronged with people glad and well nourished.
entries.92.14: And those great-souled sages there who were long of life did not remember such a sacrifice, nor had there ever been one.
entries.92.15: He who had need of gold obtained gold; he who wished for wealth obtained wealth, and he who wished for jewels, jewels.
entries.92.16: Of silver and of gold, of gems and of garments given without ceasing, a heap was to be seen.
entries.92.17: 'Not of Shakra, nor of the lord of wealth, nor of Yama or of Varuna, has such a thing been seen by us before' — so said those rich in penance.
entries.92.18: Everywhere the monkeys stood, and everywhere the rakshasas; and with full hands they gave abundantly garments and wealth and food to those who asked.
entries.92.19: Such was that sacrifice of the lion among kings, endowed with every virtue; and it went on for a full year and more, and did not fall away.
entries.93.1: While that most wonderful sacrifice was going on, Valmiki the bull among sages came swiftly with his disciples.
entries.93.2: And seeing that sacrifice of divine seeming and wonderful to look upon, he made fair leaf-huts in a place apart from the dwellings of the sages.
entries.93.3: And he had many carts, full of fruit and root and fair to see, set down not far from that lovely enclosure of Valmiki.
entries.93.4: And being greatly honoured by the king and by the great-souled sages, Valmiki of very great splendour, wholly self-possessed, dwelt there.
entries.93.5: And he said to his two glad disciples: 'Go, both of you, with full attention, and sing the whole poem of the Ramayana with the greatest joy.
entries.93.6: 'In the holy enclosures of the sages and in the dwellings of the brahmins, in the streets and upon the royal roads and in the houses of kings;
entries.93.7: 'and at the door of Rama's dwelling, where they perform the rite, and before the officiants — there above all it is to be sung.
entries.93.8: 'And here are fruits of many kinds and sweet, grown upon the crests of the mountains; taste them and sing.
entries.93.9: 'You shall come to no weariness, my children, having eaten those fruits, and roots well cleansed. You shall stay outside the city.
entries.93.10: 'And if Rama the lord of earth should call you for the hearing, then let the singing begin before the sages seated there.
entries.93.11: 'Twenty cantos are to be sung in a day in a sweet voice, with the many measures there as I have shown you before.
entries.93.12: 'And no greed at all is to be shown, not the least, out of longing for wealth. What has wealth to do with those who dwell in a hermitage and live upon fruit and root?
entries.93.13: 'And if Kakutstha should ask you, "Whose are you, boys?" — say thus to that lord of men, "We two are Valmiki's disciples."
entries.93.14: 'These strings are most sweet, and the place too is of a seeming never seen before. Give the notes their turns and sing most sweetly, free of fever.
entries.93.15: 'It is to be sung from the beginning, and the king is not to be slighted; for by dharma a king is the father of all beings.
entries.93.16: 'So do you two, with glad minds, be ready tomorrow at dawn and sing that sweet song joined with string and rhythm.'
entries.93.17: Having thus instructed them at length, that greatly renowned and most generous sage, the son of Prachetas, sat silent.
entries.93.18: And being so instructed by that sage, those two sons of Maithili, subduers of foes, went out saying, 'Even so we shall do.'
entries.93.19: And setting in their hearts that wondrous speech uttered by the sage, those two boys passed the night together in great eagerness, as the two Ashvins with the collection of Bhargava's policy.
